messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raj was a forty-nine-year-old military medic, a man who had spent two decades patching up soldiers in the field, but he could not stitch together what had happened in his own home. The abuse came from his former partner, a woman he had loved, during a violent argument after a deployment. She had hit him repeatedly with a closed fist while he lay on the floor, the smell of her sweat sharp in his nostrils, the fabric of her shirt—a particular dark blue—pressing against his face. He did not fight back; he was a medic, trained to preserve life, and the shame of that helplessness set like concrete. When the police arrived, they treated it as a domestic dispute and left without charges. His own family, when he told them, told him to keep it quiet. No one was held accountable, and Raj began to believe that something must be fundamentally wrong with him for this to have happened.

Now, years later, that belief had calcified. The smell of sweat or body odour—on a bus, in a waiting room—could send the memory flooding back, and with it came the physical pain in his ribs and jaw, as if the blows were landing again. He could not put the event into words; when he tried, the words dissolved, and the reliving took over entirely. He felt it happening right now, the helplessness and the sting. Because he believed he was defective, he interpreted the reliving as proof: *see, you are broken*. That appraisal, in turn, made him feel that nothing in his life held meaning anymore—his work as a medic felt hollow, his current marriage distant.

To manage the threat, Raj had narrowed his world. He struggled to fall asleep because he needed to stay alert; he would lie rigid in bed, listening to the creaks of the house, starting at the hum of the furnace. Only a very limited number of places felt safe—his locked bedroom, and sometimes his car. The hypervigilance itself made him more sensitive to triggers: he would jump at ordinary sounds, and that jumpiness would then bring the memory rushing back, a loop tightening. He avoided wearing clothes similar to the dark blue shirt his ex-partner had worn, discarding three shirts from his wardrobe. He stopped exercising altogether because the physical exertion, the sweat and the pounding heart, mimicked the fight response and triggered the pain recall. He avoided other people as much as possible. When he saw police officers—authority figures who had failed him—his chest would tighten, and the negative appraisal of *no accountability* would surge, driving him further into isolation. The avoidance itself reinforced his defectiveness: by withdrawing, he convinced himself he could not function normally.

The causal connections felt like a closed system. A trigger—say, the sharp scent of sweat in a grocery store aisle—would activate the memory, which would then amplify his sense of threat, making him startle at a dropped can. That startle, in turn, renewed his negative appraisals: *I am not safe, nothing matters*. He would then cancel his plans to avoid people, and that isolation gave him more time to ruminate, bringing the memory back with sharper intensity. The threat of being seen by a known relative or a police officer made him scan every face, and that scanning itself became a trigger for the memory of his partner's face contorted in rage. Even his sleep vigilance, an attempt to feel safe, meant he was perpetually on edge, and that edge left him more vulnerable to intrusive images of the event.

He had changed his life around these patterns. As a medic, he worked in a clinic now rather than in the field, but even there he avoided the break room because the proximity of colleagues felt dangerous. He had stopped attending family gatherings, citing long shifts. His wife had begun to complain that he was distant, that he seemed afraid of everything. What frightened Raj most was the feeling that the abuse was still happening, that he was still that helpless man on the floor. He finally sought help when he realised he had begun avoiding his own reflection, a moment of clarity that something had to give. He was terrified that the therapy would confirm his defectiveness, but he was equally terrified of living the rest of his life in a shrinking box.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals directly cause or increase sense of threat.
No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals directly lead to or intensify the trauma memory.
